Criminal Appeal No. 4923 of 1991 (Dhaka)
Criminal Appeal No. 87 of 1986 (Rangpur)
lawyer:
Muhammad Ayenuddin, Advocate -------- For the Appellant.
Abdus Salam Mamun, AAG  -------- For the State.
parties:
Rajab Ali Zulfiqar  -------- Appellant.
Vs.
State   -------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. The prosecution case in brief is, that the appellant as the Head Teacher of the Bakshiganj Primary School drew an amount of Tk. 10,000.00 by cheque No. 384382 dated 2.12.82 issued by the District Education Officer as the first installment from the Bangladesh Krishi Bank, Kurigram Branch out of Government grant of Tk. 17,480.00 for the financial year 1981-82 for doing some repair and development work of the said school. Out of the said amount of Tk. 10,000.00 the appellant first deposited the cheque for the said amount of Taka 10,000.00 in the Durgapur Branch of the said Bank and thereafter withdrew and encashed a sum of Taka 9,900.00 during the period from 11.2.83 to 15.3.83 and out of the said amount he spent Tk. 3,100.00 for purchasing some wooden posts and kept the balance amount with him. The time schedule for the development work of the said school was about to expire but he could not finish the repair and development work of the said institution. Hence he was asked to finish the work of development within 14.3.83 and to submit account for the said amount of money received by him but he failed to do so. He was then given repeated pressure and reminders to repay the balance money lying with him but ultimately he paid back Tk. 3,000.00 only to the Sub-Assistant Engineer of the Ulipur Upazila Education Office and the rest sum of Tk. 3,800.00 remained with him for which he could not give any account. In that circumstance failing to realise the balance amount, the Thana Education Officer, Ulipur lodged a complaint to the District Anti-Corruption Officer, Rangpur and to the District Education Officer, Kurigram when an Enquiry Case No. 629/83 was started by the Anti-Corruption Department. The Anti-Corruption Department also received a Memo dated 19.10.83 with a paper cutting from the 'Daily Dabanal' dated 27.9.83 publishing the news of misappropriation of Government fund by the Head Master of the said primary school from the Martial Law Authority, Bogra. 

 3. The case was then enquired into by an Assistant Inspector of DAB as well as by PW 1 Md. Khandkar Nazmul Haque, (Recd.) Assistant Inspector, Kurigram who after the enquiry having found a prima facie case lodged a regular FIR on 30.9.84 with the Ulipur Police Station against the accused appellant. PW 1 himself then took up the investigation of the case, seized some alamats, examined some witnesses under section 161 CrPC and obtained sanction from the Government and then submitted charge-sheet against the accused appellant under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of Act II of 1947. Meanwhile, some departmental action was taken and the accused appellant was put under suspension. The accused appellant from the very beginning was absconding and in spite of issuance of Proclamation and Attachment and Warrant of Arrest his attendance could not be secured in court and ultimately records of the case along with charge-sheet were transmitted to the court of the learned Sessions Judge and ex-officio Sr. Special Judge, Kurigram for trial. On receipt of the case records, the learned Sessions Judge and Sr. Special Judge took cognizance of the offence against the accused appellant under section 409 of the Penal Code read with section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947. Meanwhile, to comply with the provisions of section 339B of the Code of Criminal Procedure, there was Gazette Notification and Publication in the newspaper about the trial of the accused appellant in absentia but he did not turn up. Therefore the trial Court decided to proceed with the trial of the accused appellant in absentia. The trial Court i.e. the learned Sessions Judge and ex-officio Special Judge, Kurigram then framed charge against the accused-appellant on 22.2.86 under section 409 of the Penal Code and section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 in absence of the accused appellant. 

 The learned AAG for the State, on the other hand, submits that in view of section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 the alleged offences under section 409 PC and section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 undoubtedly are schedule offences and exclusively triable by a Special Judge. But his contention is that the present case was in fact tried under the Criminal Law Amendment 1958 by an ex-officio Senior Special Judge who was at the same time a Sessions Judge and his appointment as a Senior Special Judge was notified in the official Gazette by a general notification No. 3498-J 24th October, 1958 which runs as under: 

 "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 4 of the Pakistan Criminal Law Amendment Act (now Bangladesh) 1958 (Act XL of 1958), the Government is pleased to direct that all Sessions Judges of East Pakistan and Bangladesh be the Senior Special Judges in respect of their respective Sessions Divisions". 

 According to the contention of the learned AAG, the said notification has been adopted in Bangladesh and is still in force in this country. He therefore argues that the present Sessions Judge was by operation of law a Senior Ex-officio Special Judge in his Sessions Division by virtue of the above notification and quite competent to try cases under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. He further, submits that the present case has been numbered as a Special Case as is generally done in a case under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and from the charge it also appears that the same was framed under section 409 of the Penal Code and also section 5(2) of Act II of 1947 by the Sessions Judge and ex-officio Senior Special Judges, Kurigram. But subsequently at the top of the order-sheet of the case and at the bottom of the signature of the trial Judge in his judgment the words ex-officio Senior Special Judge has not been mentioned through bonafide mistake. Therefore, the learned AAG contends that for this omission it cannot be said that the trial of the present case was not held by a special Judge under the Criminal Law Amendment, 1958. However it is his contention that the above omission is at best an irregularity which is curable under section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the same has not caused any prejudice to the accused appellant, as in the trial all other provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 have been fully complied with. Further, it is contended by the learned AAG for the State that the question of jurisdiction, if any, ought to have been raised at the earliest by the defence but in the instant case the accused-appellant remained all through in absconsion and did not feel the necessity of defending himself by appearing in the court and engaging any advocate or raising any such question of jurisdiction at the trial. So, the contention that the trial was held without jurisdiction has no substance and on that baseless plea alone the impugned conviction and sentence of the appellant should not be set aside. 

 and then submits that there is no dispute that the accused appellant was entrusted with the alleged money. Now, the only question is whether he committed criminal breach of trust, that means whether he dishonestly misappropriated or converted to his own use the said money he received or dishonestly used or disposed of the same in violation of the direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust was to be discharged or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he had made touching the discharge of such trust or willfully suffered any other person so to do. The learned AAG referring to the terms of entrustment of the alleged Government money with the accused appellant for the purpose of repair and development of the school, however submits that the money in question was a grant for the school for financial year 1981-82 and a specific time was given for its utilization, that is for the repair and development of the school, but from the evidence on record including some resolutions in the Resolution Book seized in this connection, it transpires that the accused appellant did not or could not utilize the money as granted by the Government for the repair and development of the school concerned in due course and the grant was going to be lapsed for the failure of the accused appellant to discharge his responsibility in utilizing the alleged fund for the school in due course who did not even return the said money to the proper authority, rather in spite of repeated reminders he did not care to comply with the instructions of the concerned authority and purposely defaulted in paying the money back and thus accounting for the same. The learned AAG for the State further submits, relying also on the evidence of the PWs including PWs 3 and 5 as well as on some resolutions of the managing committee of the school as contained in Ext. 4, that the accused appellant received a cheque of Tk. 10,000.00 for the repair work of the school out of which he spent only Tk. 3,100.00, for purchase of some pieces of wooden posts and returned a sum of Tk. 3,000.00 and the rest could not be accounted for and was due from him for which there was a number of reminders issued to him but without any result. The learned AAG further submits that the accused appellant misappropriated the rest amount of Tk. 3,800.00 with dishonest intention which can also be inferred from the fact that he wanted a false voucher Tk. 10,000.00 as against his purchase of wooden posts for Tk. 3,100.00 but the office refused to do so as evidenced by PW 3. Now, with regard to the ingredients of the offence under section 409 as defined in section 405 of the Penal Code, it is submitted that even if a refund of the money entrusted with is made at a later stage by the accused that will not absolve him from the charge under section 409 of the Penal Code and even if there is a temporary misappropriation of the money with dishonest intention that will bring one within the mischief of the offence under section 409 or 405 of the Penal Code. In support of his submission the learned AAG has relied on two decisions, one in the case of State Vs. Abu Raza reported in 18 DLR (SC) 512 and another in the case of State Vs. Nazir Hussain reported in 16 DLR (WP) 48.
